title: Questions to ask an R&D tax consultant during an interview
description: Key questions to ask an R&D tax credit consultant on eligibility, documentation, Form 6765 Section G, IRS examination defense and fees.
summary: This page lists the key questions U.S. businesses should ask when interviewing an R&D tax credit consultant, covering IRC § 41 eligibility, documentation, Form 6765 Section G, §§ 174A and 280C coordination, IRS examination defense and fees. The key takeaway: choose a consultant who can prove audit readiness, not just find eligible spending, and confirm commitments in writing.

body.text: This page lists the key questions U.S. businesses should ask when interviewing an R&D tax credit consultant, covering IRC § 41 eligibility, documentation, Form 6765 Section G, §§ 174A and 280C coordination, IRS examination defense and fees. The key takeaway: choose a consultant who can prove audit readiness, not just find eligible spending, and confirm commitments in writing.

Jurisdiction: United States of America (federal). Status of law and guidance reviewed: as of November 10, 2026. This report is informational only and is not legal or tax advice. Taxpayers should confirm the application of these rules to their own facts with a qualified professional.
Passages labeled Analysis are interpretation, not statements of law. Passages labeled Self-reported describe what a firm says about itself and have not been independently verified.
1. Why the Interview Questions Matter Now
Each of them affects what a competent consultant should be able to say in an interview in late 2026.
1.1 Recordkeeping standard for the research credit

Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) requires a taxpayer claiming the credit for increasing research activities under IRC § 41 to retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit. The regulation cross-references Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1 for the general record-retention rules that apply to all taxpayers. It also permits the IRS and a taxpayer to agree on guidelines for keeping specific records for purposes of substantiating research credits.

The regulation does not use the word "contemporaneous." The emphasis on contemporaneous documentation comes from practitioner commentary, notably Jacob Kushan's October 31, 2025 article in The Tax Adviser, which describes detailed project descriptions and contemporaneous records as critical to defending a research credit claim.

Analysis. The legal test is substantiation in "sufficiently usable form and detail." Contemporaneous records are not legally mandated, but they are usually the most persuasive way to meet that test, because they show what the taxpayer knew, attempted and learned at the time, rather than a reconstruction prepared after a claim is challenged. An interview question about recordkeeping should therefore ask both what records the consultant considers sufficient and how the consultant helps the client create them during the year.
1.2 Form 6765, Section G (business component reporting)

In news release IR-2025-99 (October 1, 2025), the IRS announced that Section G of Form 6765, Credit for Increasing Research Activities, would be optional for all filers for tax year 2025 (processing year 2026) while it continued stakeholder engagement, and extended the comment period on the draft instructions through March 31, 2026. The Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025, for use with the January 2025 revision of the form), which were released in final form in early February 2026, state that Section G is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026 and is required for tax years beginning after 2025. Two categories of filers are excepted from the requirement:

items: a qualified small business, as defined in IRC § 41(h)(3), that elects the reduced payroll tax credit; and

a filer that meets all three of the following conditions: total qualified research expenses (QREs) at the controlled-group level of $1.5 million or less; average annual gross receipts of $50 million or less for the three prior tax years (determined under IRC § 448(c)(3), without regard to subparagraph (A)); and reporting the research credit on an original return.

body.text: Where Section G is completed, the filer reports at least 80% of total QREs by business component, listing no more than 50 business components in descending order of QREs. The remaining components are reported in aggregate under the label "Aggregate Business Components." For each listed component, Section G calls for the component's name or identifier, the type of component (product, process or other), the software type where relevant, and QREs broken out into wages, supplies, computer rental or lease costs, and contract research.

For tax years beginning before 2026 it was optional for every filer. It becomes mandatory, subject to the two exceptions above, for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025. In practical terms, calendar-year taxpayers will face mandatory Section G reporting for the first time on their 2026 returns, filed in 2027.

Analysis. Section G changes the work product a consultant must be able to deliver. A consultant that has historically reported QREs only in total must now be able to allocate wages, supplies, computer costs and contract research to individual business components, in a way that ties back to the client's books. That is a reasonable test of operational capability in an interview.
1.3 Elimination of the LB&I Acknowledgement of Facts process

LB&I Interim Guidance Memorandum LB&I-04-0725-0008 (dated July 23, 2025, released July 25, 2025) provides for the elimination of the Acknowledgement of Facts (AOF) Information Document Request (IDR). Under the memorandum, the AOF IDR process remained available, at the taxpayer's option, through December 31, 2025, and is eliminated in 2026. The attached Internal Revenue Manual (IRM) changes took effect August 1, 2025, and the memorandum expires August 1, 2027. The same memorandum confirmed that Accelerated Issue Resolution (AIR) is available in Large Corporate Compliance (LCC) cases and updated procedures for the LB&I/Appeals Fast Track Settlement (FTS) program. Existing IDR procedures in IRM 4.46.4.7 and issue-resolution procedures in IRM 4.46.5 continue to apply.

Before its elimination, the AOF IDR was issued near the end of the examination of an issue and asked the taxpayer to acknowledge, dispute or supplement the facts the examination team intended to rely on before issuing Form 5701, Notice of Proposed Adjustment (NOPA). The IRS has said it will rely instead on issue discussions throughout the issue-development process.
The IRS name is the Acknowledgement of Facts (AOF) IDR process.

Analysis. That is a reasonable inference, but it is commentary rather than an IRS statement. It also applies most directly to LB&I examinations of larger taxpayers; smaller businesses examined outside LB&I are subject to different procedures.
1.4 International comparison

That statement comes from the Thomson Reuters article, which adds that U.S. requirements remain lighter than those of many European jurisdictions. Nothing in the interview questions below depends on it.
2. Questions on Technical Eligibility (IRC § 41(d))
Under IRC § 41(d)(1), as amended by Pub. L. 119-21 (enacted July 4, 2025, commonly called the One Big Beautiful Bill Act), "qualified research" is research:

items: (A) with respect to which expenditures may be treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174A;

(B) that is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, and the application of which is intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer; and
(C) substantially all of the activities of which constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose described in § 41(d)(3).

body.text: Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) treats the "substantially all" requirement as met only if 80% or more of a research activity, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, constitutes elements of a process of experimentation. Practitioners commonly describe these elements, together with the permitted-purpose rule, as the "four-part test." That label does not appear in the statute or regulations.

After Pub. L. 119-21, § 41(d)(1)(A) refers to domestic research or experimental expenditures under new § 174A. Research conducted outside the United States remains excluded from the credit under § 41(d)(4)(F).
Q1. How do you define and document the elimination of uncertainty for each business component?

Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3) provides that research is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information if it is intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component. Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1) states that uncertainty exists if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the product, or the appropriate design of the product. A strong answer explains how the consultant ties each business component's documented objectives to a specific uncertainty of capability, method or design, and how that uncertainty is recorded at the outset of the work rather than inferred afterward.

Analysis. Listen for whether the consultant distinguishes between business uncertainty (whether a product will sell, or whether a deadline will be met) and technical uncertainty (whether the product can be built, how, or in what design). Only technical uncertainty is relevant under the regulations.
Q2. What method do you use to substantiate a process of experimentation?

Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5) defines a process of experimentation as a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or the method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities. Because the 80% "substantially all" threshold applies, the consultant should explain how it measures the share of a business component's activities that are experimental, and on what basis (for example, cost or time) that measurement is made and applied consistently.

Analysis. Records of hypotheses, tests, results and resulting design changes are the natural evidence of a process of experimentation, but the regulation does not prescribe specific document types. A consultant who can explain its measurement basis for the 80% test, and how it handles activities that fall below the threshold (including the "shrinking-back" rule in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2), under which the test is applied to progressively smaller subsets of a business component), is demonstrating a working command of the regulation.
Q3. How do you confirm the activities are technological in nature?

Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4), information is technological in nature if the process of experimentation used to discover it fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering or computer science. Section 41(d)(4) separately excludes, among other things, research after the beginning of commercial production, adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement, duplication of an existing business component, surveys and studies (including efficiency surveys, management studies and market research), certain internal-use software, foreign research, research in the social sciences, arts or humanities, and funded research. The consultant should explain who on its team makes these classifications and what technical qualifications those people hold.
Q4. How do you isolate qualified research expenses and confirm a permitted purpose?

Under IRC § 41(b), QREs consist of in-house research expenses (wages paid for qualified services, amounts paid for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research, and, under regulations, amounts paid to another person for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research) and contract research expenses (generally 65% of amounts paid to non-employees for qualified research, with higher percentages for certain qualified research consortia and qualified small businesses, universities and federal laboratories under § 41(b)(3)). Under § 41(d)(3), research must relate to a new or improved function, performance, reliability or quality; research relating to style, taste, cosmetic or seasonal design factors does not qualify. Section 41(d)(4)(H) excludes research to the extent funded by any grant, contract or otherwise by another person or governmental entity. Ask how the consultant identifies funded research, including by reviewing customer contracts for rights and payment terms, and how it excludes non-qualifying costs.

body.text: 3. Questions on § 174 / § 174A Integration
Q5. How will you coordinate the treatment of research expenditures under §§ 174 and 174A with the § 41 credit, including the § 280C election?
That rule has been replaced for domestic expenditures. Under Pub. L. 119-21, § 70302, for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024:

items: Domestic research or experimental expenditures are deductible under new IRC § 174A(a), notwithstanding § 263. Under § 174A(c), a taxpayer may instead elect to charge them to a capital account and deduct them ratably over a period of not less than 60 months, selected by the taxpayer and beginning with the month in which the taxpayer first realizes benefits from the expenditures. The § 174A(c) election must be made by the due date of the return, including extensions; the method and period chosen must be followed in later years unless the IRS approves a change; and the election does not apply to expenditures made before the year of the election.
Foreign research or experimental expenditures remain capitalized under amended IRC § 174(a) and amortized ratably over 15 years.
IRC § 59(e), as amended, also allows an optional 10-year writeoff of expenditures otherwise deductible under § 174A(a).

Pub. L. 119-21, § 70302(f), provides transition rules, including a retroactive election for certain small businesses and an election to deduct remaining unamortized domestic amounts that were capitalized in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025.

body.text: The statute supports a period of not less than 60 months under § 174A(c) and a 10-year period (which equals 120 months) under § 59(e). These are two different provisions, not one election.

The Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025) state that the reduced-credit election under IRC § 280C(c)(2) is made on Item A of a timely filed original return (including extensions), cannot be made or changed on an amended return, and is irrevocable for that tax year. If the election is made, the regular credit is computed at 15.8% instead of 20%, and the alternative simplified credit (ASC) is limited to 79% of the computed amount. If the election is not made, the taxpayer must reduce its domestic research or experimental expenditures under § 174A (whether deducted or capitalized) by the amount of the credit. Practitioner summaries of the final instructions note that for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, the reduction is the entire gross credit amount, while the older rule, under which only the excess of the credit over the § 174 amortization amount served as the adjustment, continues to apply to tax years beginning before January 1, 2025.

The Instructions for Form 6765 direct taxpayers to Rev. Proc. 2025-28, released August 28, 2025, for the transition options in § 70302(f) of Pub. L. 119-21 and for the procedures to begin applying § 174A(a) or (c) in the first tax year beginning after December 31, 2024. Consistent practitioner summaries of the revenue procedure describe the following structure:

items: Section 3 sets out the election for eligible small business taxpayers (those meeting the § 448(c) gross receipts test, which for 2025 is average annual gross receipts of $31 million or less for the three prior tax years) to apply § 174A retroactively to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, using an election statement titled "FILED PURSUANT TO SECTION 3.03 OF REV. PROC. 2025-28."

Section 4 provides procedures for an eligible small business taxpayer to make a late § 280C(c)(2) election for prior years, and Section 5 provides procedures to revoke a prior § 280C(c)(2) election. Retroactive application of § 174A by a small business requires retroactive application of the conforming § 280C(c) amendments.
Section 6 provides procedures for the § 174A(c) election to capitalize and amortize domestic expenditures.
Section 7 modifies the automatic accounting method change procedures in Rev. Proc. 2025-23, including a small business retroactive method change that can be used in place of amended returns.

body.text: A consultant should be able to explain which of these paths, if any, applies to the client.

Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(2) explains that costs may qualify only to the extent they are incurred in activities intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty, and that costs incurred after uncertainty is eliminated, such as ordinary production costs, are not research or experimental expenditures.
Worked example (hypothetical, regular credit). A company's qualified research expenses exceed its base amount by $500,000 under the regular credit method.

items: Without the § 280C election: credit = $500,000 × 20% = $100,000, and the company's § 174A domestic research or experimental expenditures are reduced by $100,000.
With the § 280C election: credit = $500,000 × 15.8% = $79,000, and no reduction to § 174A expenditures is required.

body.text: Worked example (hypothetical, alternative simplified credit). A company's ASC computed before any § 280C election is $60,000.

items: Without the § 280C election: credit = $60,000, and § 174A expenditures are reduced by $60,000.
With the § 280C election: credit = $60,000 × 79% = $47,400, and no reduction to § 174A expenditures is required.

body.text: Analysis. A good consultant should be able to model both outcomes for the client's actual facts, including the effect on taxable income, any state conformity differences, and the timing difference between deducting and amortizing § 174A expenditures. The better choice depends on the client's marginal tax rate, loss position and credit-utilization outlook and is not determined by the examples. Because the § 280C election cannot be made or changed on an amended return, the consultant should also explain how it coordinates with the client's return preparer so that the election is made, or deliberately not made, on the original return.
4. Questions on Documentation and Audit Defense
Q6. What records do you require during the year, and how are they dated and stored before the claim is filed?

The legal standard is the Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) requirement that records be kept in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate the claim (Section 1.1). Records must also be retained for as long as they may be material to the administration of any internal revenue law, under the general rules of Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1.

Analysis. Useful follow-up questions include which systems the consultant draws evidence from (project management, version control, laboratory notebooks, engineering change orders), how the evidence is preserved, and who on the client's side is responsible for producing it.
Q7. How will you complete Form 6765, including Section G where it applies?

Ask whether the consultant can report QREs by business component in the format Section G requires (Section 1.2), including the 80% / top-50 rule and the aggregate line for remaining components, and whether it has evaluated whether the client falls within either Section G exception. The Instructions for Form 6765 state that the business component identifier used in Section G should be consistent with the books and records supporting the QREs.

For research credit refund claims made on amended returns (or administrative adjustment requests), the Instructions for Form 6765 require the information needed for a valid claim to be provided; for electronic filers, the attachment is named "Form6765ClaimInformation.pdf." IR-2025-99 extended the transition period, during which taxpayers have 45 days to perfect a research credit refund claim before the IRS makes a final determination, through January 10, 2027. Practitioner summaries of the final instructions also note that, because Section G is not required for tax years beginning before 2026, taxpayers filing refund claims for those years should continue to follow the specific-information requirements set out in IRS Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F.
Q8. How do you track wages, supplies and other qualified costs by activity?

Ask how payroll and supply data are linked to business components. The Form 6765 instructions state that a taxpayer using statistical sampling must comply with Rev. Proc. 2011-42, that filing the form does not mean the IRS accepts the sample as adequate substantiation, that a sampling taxpayer must still report business components under the 80% / top-50 rule where Section G applies, and that the sampling plan must be attached (for electronic filers, as "Form6765StatSamplePlan.pdf"). A sampling taxpayer must still keep the records required by Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) and IRC § 6001.

Analysis. A consultant that relies on estimates or interviews alone, without a documented link between time records and business components, is likely to have difficulty supporting a Section G report once it is mandatory.
Q9. What is your record in defending R&D claims under IRS examination, including LB&I examinations?

Analysis. There is no official or standardized measure of a consultant's audit success, so ask how any figure offered is defined: the number of claims examined, the share of the claimed credit sustained, the period covered, and whether the figure includes cases resolved at IRS Independent Office of Appeals or in litigation.
Q10. What is your step-by-step protocol for an IRS examination now that the AOF process is gone?

Ask how the consultant manages IDR responses, issue discussions with the examination team, any NOPA response and any appeal. Under LB&I-04-0725-0008, the AOF IDR is eliminated in 2026 (Section 1.3), and the IRS has said it will rely on issue discussions throughout the issue-development process. For LB&I taxpayers, also ask whether the consultant has experience with Accelerated Issue Resolution, which the memorandum confirmed applies to Large Corporate Compliance cases, and with Fast Track Settlement.

Analysis. The facts recorded in IDR responses and issue discussions during the examination become the main place to set out the taxpayer's version of events. A consultant should be able to explain who drafts IDR responses, who reviews them for technical accuracy, and how the consultant ensures that the record developed during the examination is complete before a NOPA is issued.

body.text: 5. Questions on Quality Control, Independence and Fees
Q11. What technical expertise is required of the reviewers on every claim?

Analysis. This follows from the technical content of IRC § 41(d) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a), which turn on engineering and scientific concepts such as uncertainty, experimentation and reliance on the hard sciences, though no rule requires a particular reviewer qualification. Separately, anyone who practices before the IRS on the client's behalf, for example by representing the client in an examination, must be authorized to do so under Treasury Department Circular No. 230 (for example, as an attorney, certified public accountant or enrolled agent). Ask who will sign the client's Form 2848, Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative, if an examination occurs.
Q12. How do you stay current on federal and state R&D incentives?

Ask the consultant which states it files in, how it tracks state conformity to the federal changes made by Pub. L. 119-21 (including §§ 174A and 280C), and how it tracks changes in federal guidance such as the Form 6765 instructions.
Q13. What objective, third-party validation exists for your risk-management processes?

The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) states that ISO 31000 cannot be used for certification purposes; it provides good-practice guidelines but is not a certifiable risk-management standard. ISO's catalog lists ISO 31000:2018, Risk management — Guidelines, Edition 2, published February 2018, as the current edition; it cancelled and replaced ISO 31000:2009 and is flagged in the catalog as an International Standard to be revised. By contrast, ISO/IEC 27001 (information security management) is a certifiable management-system standard.

Analysis. If a consultant cites an "ISO 31000 certification," ask what it means, since the standard is guidance rather than a certifiable management-system standard. If a consultant cites ISO/IEC 27001 certification, ask for the certificate, the issuing certification body and the scope of the certified system, since an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate covers only the processes within its stated scope.
Q14. What is your fee structure, and how are audit defense costs handled?
Ask whether examination defense work is included in the engagement fee, billed hourly or covered by a separate product, and get any coverage terms in writing in the engagement letter.

Treasury Department Circular No. 230, § 10.27, limits contingent fees for practice before the IRS. A practitioner generally may not charge a contingent fee for services rendered in connection with any matter before the IRS, but exceptions permit contingent fees for services rendered in connection with the IRS's examination of, or challenge to, an original return; for an amended return or claim for refund or credit filed within 120 days of the taxpayer receiving a written notice of examination or a written challenge to the original return; for a claim for credit or refund filed solely in connection with the determination of statutory interest or penalties; and for services in judicial proceedings. Federal courts have addressed the scope of IRS authority over return preparation (Loving v. IRS, 742 F.3d 1013 (D.C. Cir. 2014)), and the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia held in Ridgely v. Lew, 55 F. Supp. 3d 89 (D.D.C. 2014), that § 10.27 could not be enforced as applied to the preparation and filing of ordinary refund claims. Analysis: contingent fees for preparing research credit refund claims are therefore not clearly prohibited by Circular 230 today, but a client should understand how any success-based fee is calculated and whether it creates an incentive to overstate a claim.
Q15. What safeguards keep the calculation conservative and defensible?

Ask how the consultant decides which activities and costs to leave out, how it applies the § 41(d)(4) exclusions, who signs off on the final calculation, and whether the client receives a written explanation of the excluded items. This is a judgment question with no statutory benchmark.

Analysis. The accuracy-related penalty under IRC § 6662 can apply to an underpayment attributable to negligence or a substantial understatement, and the erroneous-claim penalty under IRC § 6676 can apply to an excessive refund claim made without reasonable cause. A consultant's explanation of its conservatism should therefore include how it documents positions so that the client can show reasonable cause and good faith if a claim is reduced.
Additional questions

items: Are you independent of our statutory auditor? For issuers subject to Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) rules, permissible non-audit services, including tax services, are not banned outright. They require audit committee pre-approval, and the PCAOB adopted rules specific to tax services, including Rule 3521 (Contingent Fees), Rule 3522 (Tax Transactions), Rule 3523 (Tax Services for Persons in Financial Reporting Oversight Roles) and Rule 3524 (Audit Committee Pre-approval of Certain Tax Services). Under Rule 3521, an auditor is not independent of an audit client if it provides any service or product to the client for a contingent fee. These rules apply to audits of public companies and other PCAOB-regulated entities, not to every business. A private company whose financial statements are audited under AICPA standards is subject to the AICPA Code of Professional Conduct, which also restricts contingent fees for attest clients.

Do you have experience in our industry? A reasonable question; there is no factual claim to verify. Ask for examples of business components the consultant has documented in the client's industry and how those components were treated under the § 41(d)(4) exclusions.
How do you determine technical eligibility? Covered by Q1 through Q4 above.

body.text: 6. Conclusion

First, domestic research or experimental expenditures are deductible again under § 174A for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, with an election to amortize over not less than 60 months, so a consultant still applying TCJA five-year amortization to domestic costs is out of date. A competent consultant should also be able to explain the Rev. Proc. 2025-28 transition options and how they interact with the § 280C election.

Second, Form 6765 Section G becomes mandatory for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025, subject to the qualified-small-business payroll election exception and the $1.5 million QRE / $50 million gross receipts original-return exception. Consultants must be able to report at least 80% of QREs by business component.
Third, the LB&I Acknowledgement of Facts IDR process is eliminated in 2026, which places more weight on the factual record developed through IDR responses and issue discussions during an examination.

Fourth, the § 280C reduced-credit election can be made only on a timely filed original return, so the consultant's coordination with the client's return preparer is itself a meaningful interview topic.
